chapter_summary:
After all your models, animations, particles, and shaders are in place, there's one final layer of visual polish that can dramatically elevate your game's aesthetic: **Post-Processing Effects**. These are full-screen image effects applied to the camera's final rendered image before it's displayed on screen. Think of it like applying filters in a photo editor, but in real-time to your game. Post-processing can enhance realism, establish mood, improve readability, and define the overall artistic style of your game.

Unity offers integrated post-processing solutions depending on your render pipeline:
*   **Built-in Render Pipeline:** Uses the `Post Processing Stack v2` package (available via Package Manager).
*   **Universal Render Pipeline (URP) / High Definition Render Pipeline (HDRP):** Post-processing is built directly into the render pipeline and configured via `Volume` components. For this course, we'll focus on the URP approach, as it's the modern standard for new Unity projects and integrates seamlessly.

To enable post-processing in URP:
1.  **Enable in URP Asset:** Select your `UniversalRenderPipelineAsset` in the Project window (usually found in a `Settings` folder). In the Inspector, ensure `Post-processing` is checked under the `Renderer Features` section.
2.  **Add `Post Process Layer` to Camera:** Select your `Main Camera` in the Hierarchy. Add a `Post Process Layer` component. Set its `Volume Layer` to a dedicated layer (e.g., create a new layer called "PostProcessing" and assign it). This layer determines which `Post Process Volume` components the camera will process.
3.  **Create `Post Process Volume`:** Right-click in the Hierarchy, select `Volume > Global Volume`. This creates a GameObject with a `Volume` component. Set its `Layer` to the same "PostProcessing" layer you assigned to the camera.
4.  **Create `Volume Profile`:** In the `Volume` component, click `New` next to the `Profile` field. This creates a new `Volume Profile` asset in your Project window. This profile is where you define all your post-processing effects.

Now, with the `Volume Profile` selected in the Inspector, you can add and configure various effects:

*   **Bloom:** Simulates the effect of extremely bright light sources bleeding over into surrounding areas, creating a soft glow. Great for sci-fi, fantasy, or stylized games. Adjust `Intensity` and `Threshold`.
*   **Vignette:** Darkens the edges of the screen, drawing attention to the center. Useful for mood, horror, or cinematic effects. Adjust `Intensity` and `Smoothness`.
*   **Depth of Field (DoF):** Blurs parts of the scene based on their distance from the camera, simulating real-world camera optics. Excellent for cinematic shots, emphasizing foreground/background, or hiding distant detail. Configure `Focus Distance`, `Aperture`, and `Focal Length`.
*   **Color Grading:** Adjusts the overall color balance, contrast, and saturation of the image. This is crucial for establishing the game's mood and artistic style (e.g., desaturated for gritty realism, vibrant for cartoonish). Use `Mode` (HDR or LDR), `White Balance`, `Tone Mapping`, `Color Wheels`, and `Channel Mixer`.
*   **Ambient Occlusion (AO):** Adds soft shadows where objects are close together, enhancing perceived depth and realism. Configure `Intensity` and `Thickness Modifier`.
*   **Screen Space Reflections (SSR):** Simulates reflections on shiny surfaces using only screen-space information. Visually impressive but can be performance-intensive.
*   **Motion Blur:** Blurs objects that are moving rapidly, simulating real-world camera motion blur. Can enhance the feeling of speed but can also cause motion sickness for some players.

**Global vs. Local Volumes:**
*   A **Global Volume** (as created above, with `Is Global` checked) applies its effects to the entire scene.
*   A **Local Volume** (with `Is Global` unchecked) requires a `Collider` component (e.g., `Box Collider`) and only applies its effects when the camera enters its bounds. This is useful for specific areas, like a dark cave or a brightly lit room, where you want different post-processing settings.

**Optimization Considerations:**
Post-processing effects are computationally expensive because they process every pixel on the screen.
1.  **Prioritize Effects:** Only enable the effects that truly enhance your game's visuals. Bloom and Color Grading are often high-impact.
2.  **Reduce Intensity:** Lowering `Intensity` values for effects like Bloom or DoF can significantly reduce their cost.
3.  **Lower Quality Settings:** Many effects have quality settings (e.g., `Resolution` for DoF, `Sample Count` for AO). Reduce these for performance.
4.  **Disable When Not Needed:** For local volumes, ensure they are only active when the camera is inside. For global volumes, consider disabling the `Post Process Layer` component on the camera if post-processing is not needed for certain scenes or low-end devices.
5.  **Profile:** Always use Unity's Profiler (`Window > Analysis > Profiler`) to identify which post-processing effects are consuming the most GPU time.

Common mistakes:
*   **Forgetting to enable Post-processing in URP Asset:** The effects won't show up.
*   **Incorrect `Volume Layer` setup:** Camera's `Post Process Layer` and `Volume` component's `Layer` must match.
*   **No `Volume Profile` assigned:** Effects are defined in the profile, not directly on the volume.
*   **`Is Global` unchecked for a global effect:** If you want scene-wide effects, ensure `Is Global` is checked on your `Volume` component.
*   **Overdoing it:** Too many effects or excessively high intensities can make your game look muddy, artificial, or even cause motion sickness. Use post-processing subtly and purposefully.

By carefully selecting and tuning your post-processing effects, you can achieve stunning visual results that truly define the look and feel of your game.

screens.title: Post-Processing Effects & Camera Enhancements
screens.subtitle: Finish your scene with real-time image effects that define mood, clarity, and style

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn why post-processing is the final, decisive layer of visual polish in a Unity scene and how it changes what players perceive. Post-processing takes the camera's final rendered image and applies full-screen adjustments — like Bloom, Vignette, Depth of Field, and Color Grading — to solve readability problems, emphasize focal points, and establish mood. We focus on the Universal Render Pipeline workflow because it bundles post-processing into Volume components that are easy to manage across scenes. You will see the concrete setup steps: enabling post-processing in the URP asset, attaching a post process layer to the camera, creating a global Volume and Volume Profile, and tuning a few high-impact effects. I will also explain when effects cost too much and how to profile them. As you follow along, think about the artistic role of each effect: Bloom intentionally exaggerates bright light, while Color Grading defines a game's color story. By the end, you will be able to set up URP post-processing in a simple scene, pick a few effective effects, and tune them to balance performance and style. Which visual feature will you adjust first to match your game's mood?

keyIdea.title: Final image polish
keyIdea.text: Post-processing is a full-screen finishing pass that turns raw renders into a deliberate, readable, and stylish image.

Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Post-Processing Overview
Post-Processing Effects & Camera Enhancements
Apply full-screen image effects to define mood, clarity, and performance trade-offs.
In this lesson

You will set up URP post-processing, create a global volume and profile, and tune Bloom, Vignette, and Color Grading for a simple scene. We'll also cover optimization and common mistakes.

Why it matters

A few well-chosen effects can dramatically improve readability and emotional impact. Misused effects can hide gameplay cues or harm performance.

Visual Concept

Color Grading

Explore Key Topics

screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives guide hands-on setup and decision-making for post-processing in URP. First, you will understand the role of post-processing: how a full-screen pass affects readability, mood, and perceived depth. This goes beyond decoration; it is a tool to solve visual problems. Second, you will be able to set up URP post-processing by enabling the feature in the URP asset, assigning a Post Process Layer on the camera, and creating a Volume and Volume Profile. That practical skill matters because the engine must be configured before effects will render. Third, you will implement Bloom, Depth of Field, Vignette, and Color Grading — knowing which parameters to tweak and what visual problems each effect solves. Finally, you will optimize settings so effects look good without overloading the G P U. You will practice reducing quality, lowering intensities, or disabling effects on low-end devices. Each objective includes a small competency milestone you can verify in your project, so you leave with demonstrable setup and tuning skills.

screens.title: What is Post-Processing?
screens.subtitle: A precise definition and how it affects the final image

narration.text: Post-processing is a full-screen image pass applied after the scene is rendered but before the pixels reach the display. Practically, that means the camera hands the final color buffer to a set of image operations — blurs, color transforms, and compositing — that alter every pixel. This layer is powerful because it operates on the whole image and can correct or accentuate visual signals. For example, Bloom simulates bright light leaking into neighboring pixels to suggest intense luminance, while Color Grading shifts white balance and contrast to establish a consistent mood. A concrete example: in a URP test scene, place an emissive cube and a dim environment. Adding Bloom with modest intensity will make the cube read at a distance, guiding the player's eye. A common misconception is that post-processing is purely decorative; in fact it solves concrete problems like low contrast, distracting detail, or lack of cinematic focus. Key takeaway: post-processing is a final design tool — use it intentionally to solve problems and communicate game information rather than to hide rendering issues. What is Post-Processing? means post-processing applies full-screen image operations to the camera's final render to shape mood and clarity.. In practical terms, a precise definition and how it affects the final image. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Post-processing applies full-screen image operations to the camera's final render to shape mood and clarity.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › What is Post-Processing?
Formal definition

Post-processing runs after the scene is rendered and modifies the final image using full-screen effects. It changes per-pixel color, brightness, and sampling to achieve visual goals.

Why it matters
It unifies tone and readability, corrects exposure, and provides cinematic control without reauthoring assets.
Concrete example
Add an emissive cube and enable Bloom in a URP profile to make the cube appear to glow at distance.
Misconception
Post-processing is not just decoration; it solves contrast and focus issues and can hide rendering problems if misused.
Visual examples
Before
Raw render without post-processing: flat contrast, less emphasis on light sources, and uniform sharpness across depth.
After
With Bloom and Color Grading: light sources read better, colors support mood, and focus can direct player attention.
Key Takeaway

Treat post-processing as a targeted tool: pick effects that solve a visual problem, test in Play mode, and verify with the Profiler for performance cost.

screens.title: Enable Post-Processing in URP & Camera Setup
screens.subtitle: The concrete, step-by-step pipeline configuration you must perform

narration.text: Before any effects will appear, URP must be configured and the camera must be told which volumes to process. Start by selecting the UniversalRenderPipelineAsset in your Project settings and enable post-processing in the Renderer Features or equivalent toggle — without that, the pipeline will skip post-process passes. Next, select your Main Camera and add a Post Process Layer component. Create a dedicated layer named PostProcessing and set the camera's Volume Layer to that layer so the camera knows which Volumes to read. Then in the Hierarchy create a Global Volume (Volume > Global Volume), set its Layer to PostProcessing, and click New to create a Volume Profile asset. In that profile you will add overrides for Bloom, Vignette, and Color Grading. A concrete example: create an emissive cube in the scene, add a Global Volume with Bloom intensity at 0.8, then enter Play mode to confirm the glow registers. A common mistake is mismatched layers: if the camera and volume are on different layers, nothing is processed. Takeaway: configuration order matters — pipeline switch, camera layer, volume with profile — and verify each step in Play mode.

keyIdea.title: Pipeline checklist
keyIdea.text: Enable post-processing at the URP asset, assign Post Process Layer to camera, create a Volume and a Volume Profile.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › URP Setup Steps
Step-by-step checklist
  1. 1. Enable Post-processing in your UniversalRenderPipelineAsset.
  2. 2. Add a Post Process Layer component to Main Camera and create a layer named "PostProcessing".
  3. 3. Create a Global Volume, set its Layer to PostProcessing, and click New to make a Volume Profile.
  4. 4. Open the Volume Profile and add effect overrides such as Bloom and Color Grading.
Common mistake: forgetting the pipeline-level toggle or having mismatched Volume Layer assignments.
Live example to try
Create a small scene with a ground plane and an emissive cube. Add a GlobalPostProcessVolume, enable Bloom with intensity 0.8 and threshold 1.0. Enter Play mode and adjust intensity to see the glow in real time.
Check
Is the Bloom visible? If not, re-check URP asset and Volume Layer settings.
Tip
Edit the Volume Profile while Play mode is running to preview real-time changes.
Key Takeaway

Follow the setup order and verify each step: pipeline, camera, layer, volume, profile. Mismatches at any stage prevent effects from appearing.

screens.title: Bloom — parameters and best practices
screens.subtitle: How to make bright elements glow without washing out your scene

narration.text: Bloom creates a soft glow around very bright parts of the image, simulating light scattering in real optics. It is controlled by parameters like Intensity, Threshold, and Scatter. Intensity scales the effect, Threshold determines which brightness levels bloom, and Scatter controls how far the glow spreads. A useful example is an emissive object: set Threshold so only the emissive parts bloom, then increase Intensity until the glow reads at distance without losing contrast. A common misconception is to crank Intensity to make the scene look dramatic — that often reduces contrast and hides important detail. Instead, use subtle bloom with a carefully chosen threshold and lower intensity. For stylized projects, a slightly stronger bloom can define a fantasy or sci-fi look, but in realistic projects keep it restrained. Key practical tip: test Bloom in a range of scene exposures and on low-end hardware, because it is applied per-pixel and can be costly. Your takeaway: bloom is high-impact but must be tuned for threshold and intensity to preserve clarity. Bloom — parameters and best practices means use threshold to limit bloom to bright sources and moderate intensity to avoid washing out contrast.. In practical terms, how to make bright elements glow without washing out your scene. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bloom tuning
keyIdea.text: Use threshold to limit bloom to bright sources and moderate intensity to avoid washing out contrast.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Bloom Details
Parameters
  • Intensity: amount of glow applied.
  • Threshold: minimum brightness to trigger bloom.
  • Scatter: spread radius of the glow.
Example: set Threshold to 1.0 so only emissive and very bright pixels bloom. Try Intensity between 0.5 and 1.0 as a starting point for stylized scenes.
Misconception: high intensity always improves visuals — instead it often flattens mid-tones and conceals detail.
Practical checklist
Test on emissive objects
Add an emissive material and tune Threshold until only the intended highlights bloom.
Balance with Color Grading
Reduce scene exposure or adjust post-exposure so Bloom doesn't dominate the frame.
Performance note
Bloom can be expensive; lower its resolution or intensity on low-end devices.
Key Takeaway

Bloom is powerful for drawing attention to bright sources. Use threshold and moderate intensity to preserve scene contrast and test performance impact.

screens.title: Depth of Field vs Vignette
screens.subtitle: How DoF and Vignette serve different storytelling goals

narration.text: Depth of Field and Vignette are both tools for guiding player attention, but they operate differently and have distinct costs and uses. Depth of Field blurs parts of the scene based on distance from the camera using parameters like Focus Distance, Aperture, and Focal Length. It's ideal for cinematic shots or to emphasize a foreground object while obscuring background detail. For example, set Focus Distance to your protagonist and increase Aperture to soften the background during a cutscene. Vignette darkens the screen edges and is extremely cheap; it quickly draws the eye to the center without changing geometry. For a horror scene, pair a stronger vignette with desaturated Color Grading to create claustrophobia. A common misconception is that DoF and Vignette are interchangeable: they are not. DoF changes perceived depth at visual cost and can be expensive depending on quality and resolution, while Vignette is a subtle tonal tool with minimal performance impact. Takeaway: use Vignette for inexpensive focus framing and Depth of Field when optical realism or cinematic emphasis is required, but always test DoF performance on target devices.

keyIdea.title: Different focus tools
keyIdea.text: Use Vignette for cheap framing; use Depth of Field for optical focus and cinematic separation, mindful of cost.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › DoF vs Vignette
Depth of Field (DoF)
Simulates camera focus using Focus Distance, Aperture, and Focal Length. Use for cinematic emphasis and to hide distant detail.
Example: Fix focus on a character in close-up; blur the background to hide unimportant geometry.
Misconception: DoF is always subtle — aggressive DoF can make gameplay feel sluggish or cause motion sickness.
Vignette
Darkens the image edges to center attention. Cheap and effective for mood and framing; works well in horror and cinematic scenes.
Example: Increase Vignette intensity slightly in a dark corridor to focus the player's sightline.
Performance: Minimal cost; safe to enable on most target devices.
When to choose DoF
Cinematic shots, portrait close-ups, or when depth separation improves narrative clarity.
When to choose Vignette
Quick framing, horror mood, inexpensive focus emphasis.
Key Takeaway
Use Vignette as an inexpensive framing tool and DoF for optical realism; test DoF performance carefully.

screens.title: Color Grading, AO, SSR & Motion Blur
screens.subtitle: Capabilities, artistic use, and performance trade-offs

narration.text: Color Grading controls the global color palette, contrast, and tone mapping. It is central to a game's identity: desaturated tones suggest grit, warm shifts feel cozy, and stronger contrast emphasizes detail. Use Color Grading modes and White Balance to fine-tune mood; for example, set a slight negative temperature for a cooler, tense scene. Ambient Occlusion adds contact shadows where objects meet to increase perceived depth. It is subtle but effective; lower sample counts to improve performance. Screen Space Reflections create reflections using only visible pixels — visually impressive on wet or shiny surfaces but limited and costly. Motion Blur smooths fast motion and can amplify speed but may induce discomfort in some players. Concrete example: for a rainy street scene, combine Color Grading (desaturated, cooler tone), AO to deepen crevices, SSR to reflect puddles, and modest Motion Blur for camera pans. A common mistake is enabling all effects at high quality: instead prioritize Color Grading and Bloom, then selectively enable AO/SSR for key surfaces. Takeaway: match effects to your scene's visual goals and measure cost with the Profiler. Color Grading, AO, SSR & Motion Blur means prioritize color grading and bloom for mood, then selectively add ao/ssr where they meaningfully enhance visuals.. In practical terms, capabilities, artistic use, and performance trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Choose effects by goal
keyIdea.text: Prioritize Color Grading and Bloom for mood, then selectively add AO/SSR where they meaningfully enhance visuals.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Color Grading & More
Color Grading
Adjusts white balance, contrast, saturation, and tone mapping to define a scene's palette and emotional feel.
Example: Use HDR mode and ACES tone mapping to preserve highlights and create cinematic contrast.
Misconception: Color Grading fixes poor asset colors — instead, it unifies and stylizes assets that are already reasonably lit.
AO, SSR, Motion Blur
Ambient Occlusion deepens contact shadows. SSR simulates reflections using screen pixels. Motion Blur adds velocity-based blur for movement.
Performance: AO and SSR can be expensive; lower quality and sample counts on constrained hardware.
Use case: SSR is worth enabling where shiny surfaces are central to the scene, like a wet street in a night scene.
Practical tip
Tune Color Grading first because it changes perception of other effects; small exposure changes can reduce need for strong Bloom.
Optimization
Lower AO sample counts, reduce SSR resolution, and selectively apply Motion Blur only to camera or high-velocity objects.
Key Takeaway
Prioritize Color Grading and Bloom for immediate mood improvements; use AO/SSR/Motion Blur sparingly and profile their cost.

screens.title: Global Volume vs Local Volume
screens.subtitle: How volumes control where and when effects apply

narration.text: Volumes define spatial rules for post-processing. A Global Volume with Is Global checked applies its effects everywhere, which is ideal for scene-wide color grading and default look. A Local Volume is unchecked for Is Global and requires a Collider to define its bounds; effects only apply when the camera enters the collider. Use Local Volumes to create area-specific looks — for example, entering a cave might reduce exposure, increase Vignette, and change Color Grading to colder tones. A concrete workflow: create a Local Volume with a Box Collider scaled to the cave interior, set Layer to PostProcessing, and tune the Volume Profile to the desired mood. Common mistakes include forgetting to set the Volume's Layer to match the camera's Volume Layer and forgetting the collider on local volumes. Architecturally, volumes let you compose layered looks: multiple volumes can blend based on priority and distance, allowing smooth transitions. Takeaway: choose Global Volumes for base visuals and Local Volumes to create contextual, area-specific effects that enhance immersion. Global Volume vs Local Volume means global volumes apply scene-wide; local volumes apply only inside colliders, enabling contextual visual changes.. In practical terms, how volumes control where and when effects apply. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Volume control
keyIdea.text: Global Volumes apply scene-wide; Local Volumes apply only inside colliders, enabling contextual visual changes.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Global vs Local Volumes
Global Volume
When Is Global is checked, the Volume's Profile applies to the entire scene unconditionally. Use it for base look and overall color grading.
Example: A GlobalPostProcessVolume sets default Bloom and Color Grading for the whole level.
Misconception: local volumes override global ones completely — they blend based on blending parameters and priority.
Local Volume
Local Volumes need a Collider and apply only when the camera is inside. Use them for environment-specific looks like caves or interiors.
Example: a cave interior local Volume lowers exposure, increases Vignette, and adds cool color grading.
Common mistake: forgetting to set the Volume's Layer to the camera's Volume Layer or omitting the collider entirely.
Blend and priority
Volumes blend by weight and respect priority. Use priorities to control which volume dominates overlapping areas.
Collider requirement
Local volumes require a collider to define bounds. Use triggers for smooth entry and exit.
Key Takeaway
Use Global Volumes for base looks and Local Volumes to provide contextual, area-specific visual changes that enhance immersion.

screens.title: Performance & Optimization Strategies
screens.subtitle: How to measure cost and reduce post-processing overhead

narration.text: Post-processing affects every pixel, so it can be expensive. The right workflow is: measure, prioritize, then reduce. Use Unity's Profiler to capture a frame and inspect G P U timings for post-processing passes. Identify which effects consume the most time — AO and SSR are frequently costly, Depth of Field can be expensive at high resolution, and Motion Blur may add per-object overhead. Prioritize the effects that give the highest visual return: Color Grading and modest Bloom often provide large impact for low cost. Then reduce cost by lowering quality settings: reduce resolution for DoF or SSR, lower sample counts for AO, and reduce bloom resolution or intensity. Another technique is conditional enabling: disable expensive effects on mobile or low-end quality levels, or enable them only inside Local Volumes when needed. Concrete example: if AO adds 6ms G P U time, reduce samples or disable it in low-quality settings and rely on baked ambient occlusion in lighting. Misconception: optimization must cut effects entirely — instead, tune parameters and resolutions first. Takeaway: always profile and prefer parameter tuning over wholesale removal when possible.

keyIdea.title: Measure then tune
keyIdea.text: Use the Profiler to find expensive effects, then reduce quality, resolution, or disable them conditionally.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Optimization Strategies
Profiling checklist
  1. Capture a frame with Unity Profiler and inspect GPU post-processing timings.
  2. Identify top-cost effects, such as AO, SSR, or high-res DoF.
  3. Tune effect parameters and test again to measure savings.
Example: if SSR costs too much on a target device, lower its resolution or disable it for that quality level.
Optimization techniques
Reduce sample counts for AO and lower SSR resolution.
Lower Depth of Field resolution or use a cheaper bokeh implementation.
Disable or reduce effects on low-end quality settings or when the camera is far from detail.
Tip

Measure cost first. Small parameter changes often yield large performance wins without losing artistic intent.

screens.title: Hands-on: Build a Simple URP Post-Processing Profile
screens.subtitle: A guided lab to add Bloom, Vignette, and Color Grading and observe results

narration.text: This lab guides you through a compact setup you can finish in minutes. Begin with a simple 3D scene: a plane, a few primitives, and an emissive cube. Confirm your project uses a URP asset. Step one: open the URP asset and enable post-processing. Step two: select Main Camera, add a Post Process Layer, and set Volume Layer to a new layer called PostProcessing. Step three: in the Hierarchy create a Global Volume, set its Layer to PostProcessing, check Is Global, and click New to create a ScenePostProcessProfile. Step four: with the profile selected, Add Override > Post-processing and choose Bloom; set Intensity to 0.6 and Threshold to 1.0. Add Vignette with Intensity 0.35 and Smoothness 0.5. Add Color Grading in HDR mode, choose ACES tone mapping, slightly reduce Post-exposure, and lower Saturation to taste. Run Play mode and tweak values in real time. A common mistake is editing the wrong Volume Profile asset — verify the Global Volume's Profile field points to the one you are adjusting. Takeaway: small, iterative changes while the game runs let you find a balanced look quickly.

keyIdea.title: Lab flow

Starter scene checklist

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to carry forward

narration.text: These are the essential ideas to remember as you work with post-processing in URP. First, post-processing is a full-screen pass that shapes mood, focus, and clarity. Treat it as a final design tool and use it to solve specific visual problems rather than to hide rendering issues. Second, URP exposes post-processing through Volumes and a Post Process Layer on the camera — ensure the pipeline-level post-processing toggle is enabled and that the camera and volumes share the same layer. Finally, balance artistic impact and performance: prioritize effects like Color Grading and Bloom for strong gains, and profile heavy effects such as AO, SSR, and high-resolution DoF. Always measure cost with the Profiler and prefer parameter tuning to wholesale effect removal when possible. Keep these principles in mind and you will create consistent, performant visuals.

keyIdea.text: Post-processing shapes final image, requires correct URP setup, and must be balanced with profiling and optimization.

Full-screen finishing pass

URP Volumes & Layers

Measure & optimize
Profile to find costly effects and tune resolution, samples, or quality levels instead of blind removal.
Takeaway

Use post-processing intentionally: configure URP correctly, pick high-impact effects, and profile to keep visuals performant and clear.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three short reminders to use during development

narration.text: Keep these three short reminders close while designing visuals. First, 'Set the pipeline' — if the URP asset's post-processing flag is off, nothing will render. Second, 'Layer alignment' — camera Post Process Layer and Volume Layers must match for effects to apply, and local volumes need colliders. Third, 'Profile first' — always use the Profiler to measure the cost of AO, SSR, and DoF before deciding to keep or tune them. These reminders help you avoid the most common setup and performance pitfalls. When in doubt, iterate small parameter changes while running the scene and compare the visual result and profiler metrics. This approach keeps your artistic intent intact while staying within performance budgets. Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Quick Reference
Enable the pipeline
Confirm the post-processing option is enabled in your UniversalRenderPipelineAsset before doing any other setup.
Match layers
Set the camera's Volume Layer to the same layer used by your Global and Local Volumes to ensure effects apply.
Profile changes
Measure GPU cost and prefer parameter tuning or conditional disabling over blunt removal of effects.
Final thought

A little post-processing goes a long way. Configure carefully, tune deliberately, and measure impact to produce beautiful, playable scenes.
